title: Introduction to Life Assurance: Concepts and Terminology

questions.stem: ‘Life assurance’ is traditionally distinguished from ‘life insurance’ because:

opts.x: Life assurance is regulated by NAICOM; life insurance is not.
Life assurance covers an event that will certainly occur (death); life insurance covers a contingent event.
Life assurance is only available on a group basis.
Life assurance premiums are always lower.

questions.answer: (B) Life assurance covers an event that will certainly occur (death); life insurance covers a contingent event.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

The traditional technical distinction: ‘assurance’ applies to events that are certain to occur (death is inevitable — the uncertainty is only of timing); ‘insurance’ applies to events that may or may not occur. Whole life and term assurance products cover death — hence ‘assurance.’ In practice, NIIRA 2025 and the Nigerian market use ‘life insurance’ as the umbrella term for all products, and the distinction is primarily pedagogical at CIIN Foundation level.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Both life assurance and life insurance products are regulated by NAICOM — the regulatory scope is not the differentiating factor.

(C) Life assurance products are available on both individual and group bases. The distinction is not about the class of policyholder.

(D) Premium levels are determined by actuarial factors (mortality risk, policy term, sum assured) — not by whether the product is called ‘assurance’ or ‘insurance.’

questions.stem: Under NIIRA 2025, the four classes of life insurance business are:

opts.x: Term; whole life; endowment; annuity.
Individual life; group life; annuity; health insurance.
Life; fire; marine; motor insurance.
Individual life; group life; credit life; microinsurance.

questions.answer: (B) Individual life assurance; group life assurance; annuity; health insurance.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

NIIRA 2025 classifies life insurance business into four statutory classes: individual life, group life, annuity (including retirement income products), and health insurance. These are the regulatory categories that determine licensing requirements, product approval processes, and capital treatment. All licensed life insurers must specify which classes of life insurance business they intend to write.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Lists product types within individual life insurance (term, whole life, endowment) rather than the statutory regulatory classes.

(C) Includes general (non-life) insurance classes (fire, marine, motor) which are classified as general insurance, not life insurance, under NIIRA 2025.

(D) Lists specific product categories (credit life, microinsurance) which are sub-types within the four statutory classes, not separate classes.

questions.stem: The sum assured in a life assurance policy is BEST described as:

opts.x: The maximum amount payable, subject to actual financial loss.
The total of all premiums paid.
The pre-agreed contractual payment on the specified event, regardless of actual financial loss.
The surrender value at maturity.

questions.answer: (C) The pre-agreed contractual payment on occurrence of the specified event, regardless of actual financial loss.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

The sum assured is fixed at policy inception by agreement between insurer and insured. On the occurrence of the insured event (death, critical illness, or survival to a defined date), the insurer pays the sum assured unconditionally — no proof of financial loss is required. This distinguishes life assurance from indemnity insurance and reflects its character as a contract of financial provision.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) describes how indemnity insurance works — payment capped by actual loss. Life assurance pays the agreed sum regardless of the loss actually suffered.

(B) Total premiums paid is the policyholder’s cost, not the insurer’s promised benefit. The sum assured is typically many multiples of total premiums (which is what makes life insurance economically valuable).

(D) The surrender value is the amount available if the policy is terminated early and is always less than the sum assured (it does not include future profit margin). It is not the sum assured.

questions.stem: A life assurance policy lapses when:

opts.x: The life assured reaches age 65.
A claim is made on the policy.
The premium is not paid within the grace period after the due date.
The sum assured exceeds ₦10 million.

questions.answer: (C) The premium is not paid within the grace period after the due date.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

Lapse is the termination of an insurance policy due to non-payment of premium. Policy conditions typically allow a grace period (commonly 30 days) after each premium due date before a life policy lapses; NIIRA 2025 does not fix a statutory minimum. If no payment is received within the grace period, the policy lapses and cover ceases. A lapsed policy may be reinstated, subject to the insurer’s reinstatement terms (usually requiring evidence of continued insurability and payment of outstanding premiums with interest).
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) A defined age (65) does not automatically lapse a policy. Some policies (e.g., whole life) continue indefinitely; others expire at a contractually defined term that may or may not be age-linked.

(B) Making a claim does not lapse a policy; it triggers the claims assessment process. If a valid claim is paid (death benefit or maturity benefit), the policy terminates naturally by payment — this is not lapse.

(D) There is no sum assured threshold that triggers lapse. Large sum assured policies simply require more underwriting evidence, not termination.

questions.stem: A reversionary bonus declared on a participating life assurance policy:

opts.x: Is paid in cash to the policyholder immediately upon declaration.
Is added to the sum assured and paid at the time of a valid claim; once declared, it is guaranteed.
Is discretionary and may be withdrawn by the insurer at any time.
Applies only to term assurance policies.

questions.answer: (B) Is added to the sum assured and paid at the time of a valid claim; once declared, it is guaranteed.

why.h: Why (B) is Correct

A reversionary bonus is a guaranteed annual addition to the sum assured of a with-profits life policy. Once the actuary declares the bonus for a given year, it is irrevocably added to the sum assured of each eligible policy and becomes a guaranteed contractual obligation of the insurer. It is not paid in cash at declaration — it accumulates and is paid as part of the total benefit at death or maturity.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Cash payment at declaration describes an interim dividend or terminal bonus mechanism, not a reversionary bonus. Reversionary bonuses are deferred — paid at the time of claim, not at declaration.

(C) Is incorrect — once declared, a reversionary bonus is guaranteed and cannot be withdrawn. This guaranteed nature is the key feature that distinguishes reversionary bonuses from terminal bonuses (which are discretionary and declared only at the time of claim).

(D) Reversionary bonuses apply to participating (with-profits) policies — typically whole life and endowment policies. Pure term assurance, being a non-participating product with no savings element, does not carry reversionary bonuses.

questions.stem: The paid-up value of a life policy is:

opts.x: Equal to total premiums paid plus interest.
The surrender value if the policy is terminated early.
The reduced sum assured at which the policy continues without further premiums, proportionate to premiums paid.
The maturity benefit payable on survival to end of term.

questions.answer: (C) The reduced sum assured at which the policy continues without further premiums, proportionate to the premiums actually paid.

why.h: Why (C) is Correct

Paid-up status is an option available to policyholders who can no longer afford premiums but do not want to surrender their policy entirely. On electing paid-up status, the policy continues in force — the life cover and savings element are maintained — but the sum assured is reduced to reflect the premiums already paid as a proportion of total premiums that would have been paid over the full term. No further premiums are required. The paid-up policy retains its death benefit (at the reduced sum assured) and, for participating policies, may continue to attract (lower) bonus additions.
Why the Others Are Wrong

(A) Describes a savings account with interest accumulation — not an insurance concept. Premiums in life insurance are not ‘invested’ and returned with interest; they fund a risk transfer.

(B) describes the surrender value — the cash amount the insurer pays if the policy is cancelled entirely and the insured walks away. Unlike paid-up conversion (where the policy continues at a reduced sum assured), surrender terminates the policy completely.

(D) describes the maturity benefit for a policy that has run its full term with all premiums paid. The paid-up value is a reduced benefit for partial premium payment, not the full maturity value.

questions.stem:
Adaeze holds a 20-year participating endowment policy with a sum assured of ₦5 million. After 12 years, accrued reversionary bonuses amount to ₦840,000. She can no longer afford the premiums.
(a) Calculate the paid-up sum assured if the policy's paid-up value table specifies a paid-up factor of 0.65 applied to the basic sum assured proportionate to premiums paid.
(b) Explain the difference between a paid-up conversion and an outright surrender, and advise Adaeze on which option is likely to be more financially advantageous given that the surrender value at this point is ₦3.2 million (including bonus surrender value).

model.h: Part (a) — Paid-Up Sum Assured Calculation

Formula: Paid-up sum assured = Paid-up factor × Basic sum assured × (Premiums paid / Total premiums payable)

Inputs:
• Paid-up factor: 0.65
• Basic sum assured: ₦5,000,000
• Premiums paid: 12 years (out of 20)
• Proportionate fraction: 12 / 20 = 0.60

Paid-up basic sum assured: 0.65 × ₦5,000,000 × 0.60 = ₦1,950,000

Bonus treatment: Accrued reversionary bonuses of ₦840,000 are typically maintained in full on paid-up conversion (they are already guaranteed). Therefore:

Total paid-up benefit at claim: ₦1,950,000 + ₦840,000 = ₦2,790,000

This ₦2,790,000 is payable at maturity (year 20 — i.e., 8 years from now) or on death during the remaining term, whichever occurs first.
Part (b) — Paid-Up Conversion vs Surrender: Comparison and Advice

Surrender: Adaeze receives ₦3,200,000 (including bonus surrender value) in cash immediately. The policy is fully terminated. All future benefit entitlement ceases.

Paid-up conversion: Adaeze receives no cash now. The policy continues, with ₦2,790,000 payable at maturity (year 20) or on death. No further premiums are required.

Financial comparison:
• Surrender delivers ₦3.2m now — higher immediate cash value.
• Paid-up conversion delivers ₦2.79m in 8 years — lower nominal value, but available only at maturity or death.
• Net present value comparison: at an assumed 10% discount rate, ₦2.79m payable in 8 years has a present value of approximately ₦1.3m — significantly below the ₦3.2m surrender value.

Protection consideration: The paid-up policy maintains ₦2.79m life cover for the remaining 8 years. This has real economic value if Adaeze has dependants — value that the surrender comparison ignores.

Advice to Adaeze: If she has an immediate cash need (emergency expenses, debt repayment, business investment) and does not have dependants who would suffer significantly from losing the life cover, surrender at ₦3.2m is the more financially rational choice given the discounted value of the paid-up benefit.

If she does not need cash immediately and has dependants who rely on her for financial support, paid-up conversion is preferable — she retains meaningful life cover and a deferred savings benefit without any further premium obligation.

Recommendation: Adaeze should assess her immediate liquidity needs and her dependants’ protection requirements before deciding. A financial adviser should walk her through this analysis.

questions.stem: Distinguish between a participating (with-profit) life assurance policy and a non-participating (without-profit) policy. Explain the nature of the simple reversionary bonus, the compound reversionary bonus, and the terminal bonus. Using a numerical example with a sum assured of ₦2 million and an assumed annual bonus rate of 3.5%, demonstrate the difference in policy value after 15 years between simple and compound reversionary bonus accrual.

model.h: Participating vs Non-Participating Policies

A participating (with-profit) policy entitles the policyholder to share in the insurer’s actuarial surplus through annual bonus declarations. If the insurer’s actual investment returns, mortality experience, and expense levels are better than the assumptions priced into the policy, the surplus is distributed to with-profit policyholders as bonuses.

A non-participating (without-profit) policy provides exactly the benefit stated at inception — no more. The policyholder bears neither investment upside nor downside. The insurer retains all surplus. These policies are typically cheaper in premium terms because no cost is built in for potential surplus distribution.
Three Types of Bonus

Simple reversionary bonus: Added as a flat percentage of the original sum assured each year. Example: 3.5% of ₦2,000,000 = ₦70,000 added each year. The bonus base does not grow.

Compound reversionary bonus: Added as a percentage of the sum assured plus all previously accumulated bonuses. The bonus base grows each year, creating a compounding effect. Even at the same declared rate, compound bonus produces a materially higher total value over time.

Terminal bonus: A discretionary additional bonus declared by the insurer only at the time of a valid claim (death or maturity). Not guaranteed — the insurer may increase or decrease the terminal bonus rate annually. Intended to distribute surplus profits that were not included in reversionary bonuses.
Numerical Demonstration — Simple vs Compound Reversionary Bonus

Sum assured: ₦2,000,000. Annual bonus rate: 3.5%. Period: 15 years.

Simple reversionary bonus:
Annual addition: ₦2,000,000 × 3.5% = ₦70,000 (same every year)
Total bonus after 15 years: ₦70,000 × 15 = ₦1,050,000
Total policy value at year 15: ₦2,000,000 + ₦1,050,000 = ₦3,050,000

Compound reversionary bonus:
Year 1: bonus = ₦2,000,000 × 3.5% = ₦70,000. Accumulated value: ₦2,070,000
Year 2: bonus = ₦2,070,000 × 3.5% = ₦72,450. Accumulated: ₦2,142,450
Year 3: bonus = ₦2,142,450 × 3.5% = ₦74,986. Accumulated: ₦2,217,436
[Compounding continues...]
Year 15 value: ₦2,000,000 × (1.035)^15 = ₦2,000,000 × 1.6753 ≈ ₦3,350,600

Difference: Compound bonus produces ₦3,350,600 vs simple bonus ₦3,050,000 — a difference of ₦300,600 (approximately 10% more) over 15 years.

Key insight for candidates: The compounding advantage grows with policy duration. Over a 25-year policy, the difference would be proportionately larger.

questions.stem: Explain the concept of a lien in life assurance underwriting. Under what circumstances would a life insurer impose a lien rather than decline an application? Describe the financial effect of a lien on the policyholder if the life assured dies during the lien period and if the life assured survives the lien period.

model.h: What Is a Lien?

A lien is an underwriting mechanism under which the insurer accepts a substandard life at standard premium rates but applies a fixed monetary deduction to any death benefit payable during a defined lien period. After the lien period expires, the policy continues for the full sum assured at standard terms. The term ‘lien’ is used because the deduction operates as a charge (a lien) on the death benefit during the lien period.
When a Lien Is Used Rather Than a Decline

A lien is preferred to a decline in the following circumstances:

1. Temporarily elevated but reducing risk: The applicant’s mortality risk is elevated now but is expected to reduce over time — for example, after recent surgery (recovery expected within 2 years), a newly diagnosed and recently treated condition, or significant obesity where weight loss is achievable and credible.

2. Borderline risk where decline is disproportionate: The underwriter is not comfortable accepting at full standard terms but considers outright decline too harsh given the overall risk profile. A lien provides a middle path.

3. Commercial and ethical balance: Declining an applicant who is likely to improve over time leaves them uninsured during a period when they may have the greatest need for cover. The lien allows some coverage to be provided immediately.

4. Business relationship considerations: For large or significant group schemes, flat exclusions or declines may be commercially unacceptable to the employer; a lien on individual high-risk members is less disruptive.
Financial Effect: Death During the Lien Period

If the life assured dies while the lien is in force, the beneficiary receives the sum assured minus the lien amount.

Example: ₦10,000,000 sum assured with a ₦3,000,000 lien active at the time of death.
Death benefit payable: ₦10,000,000 − ₦3,000,000 = ₦7,000,000.

The ₦3,000,000 reduction compensates the insurer for accepting a risk that was known to be substandard at inception.
Financial Effect: Survival Through the Lien Period

If the life assured survives the lien period, the lien is automatically and irrevocably lifted. The policy continues for the full sum assured (₦10,000,000 in the example) at standard terms, as if the lien had never existed.

Advantage over permanent exclusion or rating increase: The lien is transparent and time-limited — the policyholder knows exactly what will be paid if they die in the lien period and knows the full sum assured is restored if they survive. This is less harmful than a permanent exclusion (which never lifts) and cheaper than a premium loading (which continues to be paid indefinitely).

questions.stem: Critically evaluate the importance of NIIRA 2025's enhanced consumer disclosure requirements for life insurance policies in Nigeria. In your answer, describe the disclosures now mandated for life policyholders, assess the extent to which these requirements address the historical trust deficit in the sector, and identify any practical implementation challenges for insurers and intermediaries.

model.h: Essay Framework
Thesis

NIIRA 2025’s disclosure regime addresses the information asymmetry at the heart of Nigeria’s life insurance trust deficit. Well-designed disclosures can prevent the misleading sales that created the problem — but only if they reach the policyholder in a form they can understand and at a time they can use.
Mandated Disclosures Under NIIRA 2025

1. Policy document delivery: The complete policy document must be delivered to the policyholder on or before the policy commencement date. Electronic delivery is permitted where receipt is confirmed. This closes the historic gap where policyholders were covered but had never seen the document governing their coverage.

2. Benefit illustrations: All life policy applications must be accompanied by NAICOM-compliant benefit illustrations showing projected benefits at stated investment return assumptions. Critically, illustrations must also show benefits at a materially lower assumption — preventing the practice of illustrating only the optimistic scenario.

3. Surrender and paid-up value tables: The policyholder must be shown (before inception) the values they would receive at each year of the policy if they surrendered or converted to paid-up status. This prevents the shock of discovering that a policy surrendered in year 3 produces very little cash.

4. Key features document: A plain language summary of the policy’s key terms, benefits, and exclusions.

5. Charges disclosure (ILPs): For investment-linked products, all charges (allocation rate, mortality deduction, fund management fee) must be explicitly stated.

6. Cooling-off period: 21 days from delivery of the policy document to cancel without penalty.
Assessment of Adequacy for the Trust Deficit

The trust deficit was built on: policies not being delivered; benefit illustrations showing unrealistic returns; surrender values being far lower than expected; exclusions not being disclosed; and claims being contested on terms the policyholder never knew existed.

NIIRA 2025’s disclosure framework directly addresses each of these: delivery is now mandatory; illustrations must be conservative as well as optimistic; surrender tables are pre-sale disclosures; exclusions are in the key features document; and the cooling-off period provides a legal right to exit if the policyholder reviews the delivered document and finds it inconsistent with what they were told.

Theoretical assessment: A fully informed consumer who has read and understood the pre-sale disclosures, reviewed the benefit illustration, and seen the surrender value table is in a position to make a genuinely informed insurance purchase. Trust will follow from informed purchase decisions validated by actual claim payments.
Implementation Challenges

1. Literacy and comprehension: The key features document is required to be in ‘plain language’ but even plain language requires a reading standard that not all Nigerian policyholders possess.

2. Agent delivery: The disclosures are produced by the insurer but delivered by agents. An agent motivated to close a sale may not dwell on the surrender table or the low-scenario illustration.

3. Regulatory capacity: NAICOM must verify illustration compliance across all products in all NAICOM-approved product filings. The volume of work required for meaningful verification is substantial.

4. Digital delivery verification: Confirming that a WhatsApp-delivered policy document has been read and understood by a policyholder in rural Kano State is a practical challenge that the regulation does not fully address.
Conclusion

NIIRA 2025’s disclosure framework is the right architecture. Its effectiveness in rebuilding trust depends on: agent training and cultural change; NAICOM’s inspection of illustration and delivery compliance; and complementary investment in financial literacy that enables policyholders to use the disclosures they receive.

questions.stem: The money-back (anticipated endowment) policy is the dominant retail life product in the Nigerian market. Analyse the structural features that make this product commercially successful in the Nigerian context, including its design, the nature of the survival benefits, the role of reversionary bonuses, and its appeal relative to conventional savings products. In your answer, critically assess the risks and limitations of this product for both the policyholder and the insurer.

model.h: Essay Framework
Thesis

The money-back policy’s market dominance reflects a genuine alignment with the psychological and economic reality of the Nigerian consumer — but this alignment is partly a symptom of market underdevelopment rather than a sign of a well-functioning product market. For policyholders and insurers alike, the product carries risks that its commercial success tends to obscure.
Structural Features Explaining Commercial Success

1. Liquidity and visibility of return: The money-back policy pays survival benefits at defined intervals during the term (typically 20% of sum assured every 5 years). This addresses Nigerian consumers’ deep-seated suspicion that insurance ‘eats money’ without ever paying out. Each survival benefit is concrete, tangible evidence that the insurer pays — a trust signal that no amount of marketing can replicate.

2. Full death cover maintained: Despite the interim payouts, the full original sum assured remains payable on death throughout the term. This is the structural feature most valued by policyholders with dependants — they receive periodic cash and full death protection.

3. Participating structure: Reversionary bonuses add a savings growth dimension that makes the policy feel like an investment-savings product as well as insurance.

4. Agent incentive alignment: The money-back policy typically carries higher first-year premiums than equivalent term assurance, generating higher commission income. This creates an agent incentive to recommend the product, which has compounded its market dominance.

5. Adaptability to informal savings habits: The periodic survival benefit mimics the periodic payouts of popular informal savings vehicles (ajo/esusu) — making the product structure culturally familiar.
Risks and Limitations for Policyholders

1. Internal rate of return: The survival benefits, when discounted, produce a lower return than the premium outflow suggests. When policyholders are told they will ‘get their money back,’ they often do not understand that they are receiving nominal amounts without accounting for inflation erosion and opportunity cost.

2. High lapse rates: The money-back policy’s high premium structure means it is one of the first financial commitments Nigerian policyholders reduce when incomes fall. Early lapse generates a surrender value far below the premiums paid — the most trust-damaging outcome in Nigerian insurance.

3. Unsuitable for lower-income segments: The premium required for meaningful money-back coverage is beyond many Nigerians’ budgets. Selling money-back products to consumers who cannot sustain the premiums is a mis-selling risk.
Risks and Limitations for Insurers

1. Lapse risk: High first-year and early-year lapses create new business strain. The insurer has paid significant acquisition cost for policies that generate little premium income before lapsing.

2. Survival benefit liquidity management: The periodic payment obligations require careful asset-liability matching. An insurer that has not properly invested premiums to match the defined survival benefit dates faces liquidity risk.

3. Concentration risk: Over-dependence on a single product type exposes the insurer to material business risk if the money-back product falls from favour (e.g., if digital competitors offer better-value term-plus-savings products).
Conclusion

The money-back policy has earned its dominance by meeting a genuine consumer need in a trustworthy way. As Nigeria’s insurance market matures, however, better-informed consumers and digital distribution will create space for more efficient products. Insurers that continue to push money-back products into segments where they are unsuitable risk both regulatory sanction under NIIRA 2025’s TCF provisions and the mis-selling reputational damage that has historically made Nigerians reluctant to engage with insurance at all.
